Pearson’s advocacy for criminal justice reform and affordability has appealed to younger Democratic Party voters like 27-year-old Marko Jankov. But Jankov, who identifies as a Democratic Socialist, lives in a part of Memphis that was moved out of the 9th District and he said he was less motivated to vote for other Democrats when polls showed them unlikely to win. “They want to make it a psychological thing, where you think you can’t win,” Jankov said. The changes are exposing a rural-urban divide. Debby Gould, president of the non-partisan League of Women Voters of Tennessee, said voters of all backgrounds had concerns. “This is a time when we really have to strengthen urban-rural links and to come up with shared values,” she said. “Because rural voters are also feeling left out on this.” Hickey, the Williamson County Republican chair, said it was up to candidates to show they could work for all their constituents: “They’re going to have to put a lot of miles in their car.” Opening photo Elzey Avenue in Memphis, a dividing line between Congressional District 9 and Congressional District 5, following a Republican-led effort to redistrict Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Sources US Census Bureau (2020 Census redistricting data, TIGER/Line); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 congressional districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 congressional districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads). Additional contributions by Travis Hartman, Ben Kellerman and Tiana McGee Edited by Claudia Parsons, Kat Stafford and Julia Wolfe More from Reuters Graphics

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: Appetite for disruption
item.description: What connects Elon Musk’s flawed assault on US government waste with the latest attacks on Riyadh Airport? Both are a reminder of the importance of a functioning state, and the risks of economic upheaval. Plus: the financial fallout in the Gulf, and praise for messy economics.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! A week ago I [USN:L6N45V0TR TEXT:"highlighted"] some of the cracks in the foundations of the AI boom. Those fractures have widened as debt investors fret about [USN:L6N4610VQ TEXT:"neocloud data centre operators"] and Anthropic reports [USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"slowing revenue growth"]. Temporary wobble or turning point? Email me with your views. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “The US commute is becoming an antique roadshow. Squeezed by high vehicle prices and borrowing costs, drivers are buying older cars with loans that last as long as eight years.” Read more: [USN:L6N44G18H TEXT:"The $1.7 trln auto loan market heads for a crash"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK The average price of an Anthropic token has dropped 68% since the start of 2025. ([USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"The AI deflation trap"]) JPMorgan (JPM.N) added just $50 million to its allowance for consumer loan losses in the third quarter. ([USN:L6N45Z0W9 TEXT:"Jamie Dimon remains gloomy"]) Mukesh Ambani’s $102 billion Jio Platforms is set to go public on about the same valuation as rival telco Bharti Airtel (BRTI.NS) . ([USN:L6N45X01T TEXT:"IPO still makes sense"]) Qatar’s GDP is set to shrink by 16% this year. ([USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"But rebound in 2027"]) Dating app Bumble has a quarter fewer paying users than in 2024. ([USN:L6N45Z0WC TEXT:"AI to the rescue?"]) CREATIVE OBSTRUCTION In the US government they are known as bus people. These are the low-key functionaries on whom the state depends. “Bus people are people who if they are hit by a bus the government stops working,” a political operative states in Michael Lewis’s new book. Civil servants are the unlikely heroes of “ Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State ”, the author’s inside account of the assault on US bureaucracy by Donald Trump’s second administration and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The tale is something of a departure for Lewis, who has previously tended to favour plucky underdogs taking on an entrenched consensus. Think of the sceptical fund managers of “The Big Short”, or the data-obsessed baseball administrators of “Moneyball”. A decade ago, Lewis might have been more sympathetic to the ignorant laptop-wielding twentysomethings dispatched by Musk to root out waste and inefficiency in the US bureaucracy. Instead, the short-lived DOGE debacle has helped draw a definitive line under a three-decade celebration of disruption as a positive force. The word used to have mainly negative connotations. Then the tech revolutionaries of Silicon Valley grabbed the public imagination. Harvard professor Clayton Christensen lauded the power of disruption in his 1997 book “ The Innovator’s Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail ”. Suddenly, everyone with a smartphone could be a business revolutionary. Technological evangelists preached the benefits of applying the same approach to the core functions of the state: education, healthcare, defence and so on. Looking back, the surprise is how little resistance they faced. Even the 2008 financial crisis, which exposed the extreme fragility of modern banking, only encouraged more reckless experimentation with cryptocurrencies. It took a global pandemic, a trade conflict, and the knock-on effects from actual wars in Ukraine and Iran to remind many citizens of the importance of basic administrative competence. At the same time, Silicon Valley revealed its reckless instincts, which are now on daily display with each leap forward in artificial intelligence. Consumers might welcome AI agents that help them [USN:L6N45N158 TEXT:"find cheap flights"], but are unlikely to tolerate rogue bots filing false homicide tips with Philadelphia police, as Anthropic [USN:L8N45V1NQ TEXT:"admitted last week"]. Back in 2016, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman [USN:L8N19F4MY TEXT:"put on jeans and visited California"] to show his determination to modernise the kingdom. Business leaders praised his disruptive vision. Yet it’s hard to attract $100 billion a year of overseas investment when Houthi insurgents are [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"blowing up Riyadh’s main airport"]. Even executives who shrugged off the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi will avoid the Saudi capital when their own safety is in doubt. This does not mean the government is necessarily efficient. Large sovereign debts and rising interest rates give politicians a strong impulse to seek more savings. The waves of “creative destruction” that Joseph Schumpeter described back in 1942 remain a feature of capitalist economies. Yet that system also depends on the state continuing to perform a wide range of everyday functions. It’s time we spent less of our attention on the self-professed disruptors, and more of it celebrating the bus people. CHART OF THE WEEK The latest war in the Gulf is doing serious economic damage. The leading economies in the Middle East are all set to shrink this year. The hope is that a peace deal will allow for a big bounce in 2027 as oil shipments resume and tourists return. Yet a prolonged conflict could undermine the region’s plans to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, write [USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"George Hay and Afiq Fitri Alias"]. Meanwhile, the gusher of investment cash is dwindling as current account surpluses shrink. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS Did you know that almost all our data zips around the world on 600 fibre-optic cables laid on the ocean floor, most of them no wider than a garden hose? Neither did I until I read Katja Bego’s “Deep Connections: The Hidden Battles to Control Subsea Cables”, a new book about this fragile underwater network. On The Big View we discussed how subsea cables evolved, how they have been weaponised in the past, and whether the modern global network can survive rising geopolitical tensions. Imported Chinese cars are the current focus of trade tensions with the European Union. Aimee Donnellan beamed into the Viewsroom from the Paris Motor Show this week to debate the cap on Chinese imports – and whether European carmakers can survive the onslaught – with Antony Currie and Katrina Hamlin. PARTING SHOT The main surprise about this year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was that the winners did not already have one. Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were instrumental in reconciling the two main schools of the dismal science into what became known as the New Neoclassical Synthesis. This paved the way for the distillation of major economic problems into three equations, and the proliferation of models which remain influential today. Yet theoretical elegance came at the expense of practical utility, [USN:L6N45Y0MG TEXT:"argues Jon Sindreu"]. Today, a messier approach probably allows for better policymaking. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . Follow Peter Thal Larsen on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: Hargeisa like a local
item.description: Our digital journalist’s guide to camel milk tea, bustling markets and mobile money.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans “Resilience is victory,” goes a famous Somali proverb, and few places embody it like Hargeisa. Turned to rubble by intense bombings during a decade-long war with Somalia, this Somaliland city was rebuilt through domestic grit and community labour. Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991, is my home away from home. It is where my mother spent her early childhood and where some of my extended family still live. Though I was born in Bonn, Germany, and grew up in London, where I joined Reuters as a social media editor in 2019, I have regularly visited Hargeisa. Every time, I wish I had stayed longer. Hargeisa translates as “the place where hides are sold” in Somali, and livestock remains the backbone of the economy, alongside remittances. But it is also a city where old meets new: People buy and sell lambs and goats through their phones, using mobile money to pay for food, clothing and much else. Here’s how to experience Hargeisa like a local: Getting around: Somaliland is a devoutly Muslim place where days start early, with the first call to prayer before sunrise acting as a natural alarm for many residents. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. Everyone is in a rush, so be aware of your surroundings and be mindful of manoeuvring cars, buses, motorbikes and even the occasional determined man with a wheelbarrow. People shop at an open-air market along a street in Hargeisa, Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in the Freedom Square along Independence Avenue. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader pours camel milk at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader handles camel milk from a steel can at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man stands next to second-hand clothes for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traders wait for customers as they sell second-hand clothes. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman waits for customers at her open-air butchery. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader displays mobile phones for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Vehicles parked outside Durdur Business Center, along Road No 1, 26 June District. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman uses her mobile phone as she walks past the New Moon restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man uses a sewing machine at his tailoring stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Shoes are displayed for sale at the Kaboole fashion store. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man sits inside the Muddakar coffee house restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman sells fruit at an open-air grocery stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit at a coffee shop. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traffic along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed For a more local experience, take a minibus. It’s a hail and ride system, so just flag down the bus as you would a taxi, confirm it’s going to your destination, and let the driver know when you want to get off. Note that they can often be crowded. For journeys outside of the centre, take a taxi or Dhaweeye, which translates as “closer” in English. They are always nearby and easily flagged off the street. Mobile money is king: As is the case in many African cities, mobile money is the preferred payment method in Hargeisa and to pay for anything you will need your phone. You don't need internet access; just ask which code to use and for the vendor's number. You can also pay with cash, of course, but it may take a bit longer. What to eat and drink: Many people make a living by selling their wares on the street. As you walk around the city, you will be called into restaurants and street stalls, where fruit sellers pile watermelons as tall as a person, and vendors fry potatoes. Camel meat and camel milk are must-tries. Somalis have been eating camel for centuries, a tradition rooted in the land’s arid landscape. When crops and cattle perished, camels were the only ones to survive. For a traditional snack on the go, try dried camel meat, called muqmaad. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. For breakfast , people enjoy stir-fried goat, lamb or beef liver with Somali pancakes (lahoox), or a flaky flatbread with honey that goes well with shaax, a spiced, aromatic tea made with camel milk that tastes very similar to chai. A favourite lunch is fragrant Somali rice (bariis) and meat, typically tender, bone-in goat or lamb — with a banana on the side. Tea is at the heart of social life in Hargeisa, and you will regularly see people sitting outside tea houses, drinking and talking politics. With Ethiopia next door, you are never far from a good cup of coffee either. Try Social Cafe, one of several cafes in the city or, for a Somali twist, order Qaxwo, made with spices such as ginger, cinnamon and cardamom. City landmarks: The Hargeisa War Memorial features a downed Somali Air Force MiG-17 aircraft. Located in Freedom Square, it is probably the city's most recognisable landmark. The livestock market offers a glimpse into one of the city's main economic drivers, and is particularly interesting if you have never experienced the pastoral side of Somali culture. You’ll see large numbers of goats, sheep and camels being sold. Go in the morning to see it at its busiest. If you are looking for entertainment, stop by the Hiddo Dhawr Cultural Centre. Founded in 2013 by Somali singer and activist Sahra Halgan, it often features live performances of Somali music and poetry. For an authentic shopping experience, visit the Waheen Market, the city's main commercial market, where you will find everything from mattresses and glassware to gold jewellery. It’s also a great place to pick up a souvenir. One popular option is a dhill, a traditional wooden vessel used to store milk, usually adorned with leather straps and cowrie shells. Another is frankincense, an aromatic resin. Somaliland is one of the few places in the world where frankincense grows naturally. The gum is chewed for its health benefits, while the resin is traditionally burned to freshen homes and welcome guests. Finally, no visit to Hargeisa is complete without a trip to the money market, a famous open-air street market where vendors trade bricks of local currency and US dollars. There are piles of cash as far as the eye can see — but with mobile money now the first choice, who knows how long it will be there. Dress like a local: Hargeisa is a conservative place where people dress modestly. To fit in, try sporting some traditional dress. Women wear beautiful dresses called baatis with matching hijabs, often in tie-dye or other intricate designs, while men wear a sarong wrap decorated with traditional prints. When to visit: If you are visiting during the summer months, when it is hottest, expect average temperatures of around 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day. In winter, temperatures reach about 26 C (79 F) at their highest, which is considered cool. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population : 1.3 million Price of a cup of tea : $0.20 to $1.50. My go-to spot for breakfast or lunch is CFC. Great place to watch the sunset : Sarovar Hotel is located at the top of a mountain and offers an unforgettable view of Hargeisa. Largest university : University of Hargeisa, more than 7,000 students

item.title: Chuck Lorre on his reign as the ‘King of Sitcoms’
item.description: The television writer and producer behind “The Big Bang Theory” and “Two and a Half Men” reflects on his career, the key to great comedy, and why he remains optimistic about television.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift. Lorre knows something about making it happen. Dubbed the “King of Sitcoms,” he has spent decades making audiences laugh, from his early work as a writer on the hit comedy “Roseanne” to creating shows, including “The Big Bang Theory,” “Two and a Half Men,” “Mom,” and “Mike & Molly.” In his newly released memoir, “Sitcom,” Lorre turns that comic instinct on his own life, writing candidly about his missteps, while also looking back at the television successes and creative battles that shaped his career. Speaking with Reuters from Los Angeles, he discusses why character is key to great comedy, what he learned from getting things wrong, and why he’s optimistic about the TV industry’s future. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The memoir is very funny despite tackling difficult subjects, from failed marriages to addiction and Scientology. What made you want to open up about them now? From the outset, I was trying to write it as if I was having a conversation with somebody. Rather than reporting or reiterating stuff, I was trying to write it as if I was talking to the audience or talking to a person; more conversational as opposed to you know, being locked up in the prose of it all. I've been talking about these crazy chapters of my life for a long time and dear friend nudged me for at least two years to start writing it down. And once I started writing it down, I was quite pleasantly surprised. I realized it was cathartic. It was it was a little bit of therapy for me. Having finished the darned thing, what became really clear was all the missteps I've made in my life were all necessary for me to arrive at where I am, and I am deeply grateful for where I am. So the path may have been bumpy, but that's what was required. What most excites you about television right now, and what terrifies you? There's plenty in this world that is terrifying, but I wouldn't put TV in that category. Actually, I'm an optimist about how the business is changing. I've heard people complain that there's too many choices. And to me that's like, really? Does that mean when you walk into a supermarket, you complain that there's too many choices? That's got to be a good thing. When I came up in this in television, there was three and a half networks. Fox was just starting. And that was it. If those three said no, it's simply not going to happen. Now there's I don't know how many platforms capable of helping a writer (or) performer create something and perhaps get it seen by a legitimate audience. Of all the shows you’ve created, which felt most miraculous? Probably Big Bang. I mean, the first pilot was an abject failure, with the exception of (co-stars) Johnny Galecki and Jim Parsons. I had to wrap my head around the fact that it was poorly written and, when we were given another opportunity one year later, we got a chance to write a better pilot. You don't get do-overs in this business, but we did. Actress Kaley Cuoco along with the cast and writers of "Big Bang Theory" accept their award for favorite TV comedy at the 2010 People's Choice Awards in Los Angeles January 6, 2010. REUTERS/Lucy Nicholson I didn't understand what we were creating till we created it. I didn't understand how viscerally the audience was going to connect with these outliers, these brilliant but incompetent characters. What makes a great comedy? It's really very simple. It's about characters. Well-designed, thought out characters, portrayed by the right actor. I adored "Cheers" and "Seinfeld" and "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Archie Bunker," Norman Lear's stuff. I wasn't watching for the plot. The storytelling of it was secondary. It was these extraordinary characters that I loved and I wanted to see them every week. And that's how I've always approached creating television shows. Character, character, character. I don't think I could sit here and remember one storyline for "Cheers," but I never missed an episode because I wanted to see those characters. Those characters made me laugh. And I think that's the secret sauce for comedy. Obviously, when you work in the drama world, plotting is an entirely different thing. You're watching for the adventure, the hero's journey. That's a story. But even in that world, which I know very little about, I'm thinking about character. Going back to the importance of casting, you write about the resistance you faced casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly,” with one network executive pushing for a slimmer actress. How much has the industry changed, and how did you learn which battles were worth fighting? The nominees for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series (L-R) Martha Plimpton, Melissa McCarthy, Amy Poehler and Edie Faco stand on stage as they congratulate winner McCarthy from "Mike & Molly" at the 63rd Primetime Emmy Awards in Los Angeles September 18, 2011. REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni Well, the good news is, because I've had some success, I don't have that many battles anymore. But it took a long time for me to fight for who I believed in as opposed to being a good soldier and taking direction. I learned the hard way that when you do what you're told to do by others and you fail, it's your failure. It's not theirs. At a certain point, I started to dig my heels in and I think first and most formidably (was) with Jon Cryer. I talk about how much resistance I got from CBS to cast Jon in "Two and a Half Men" and then Melissa McCarthy. Here was a generational talent and it was "over my dead body" kind of casting. And I went, "Fine, well, produce a dead body because we're going over it." I guess what I'm trying to say is, it took me a while to find the courage to fight these fights. I didn't have it in the beginning. I was too frightened about being tossed aside and sent home. American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole How concerned are you about AI in the writers’ room? Are the protections won in the 2023 writers’ strike enough? There's plenty of reason to be concerned about this technology. Television would be the least of it, I would think. Why is that? I just think, if we're going to prioritize our concerns, for me AI is concerning in that it could topple civilization, not take away jobs on sitcoms, not that that's not important. But creating an intelligence that so wildly surpasses human intelligence is an incredibly risky endeavor. Look what we've done as the apex predator on this planet. Imagine what would happen if there was an apex-apex predator that viewed us the way we view insects. That scares me. Do you expect to see more shows tapping into those fears? We did an episode on "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" with an AI overlord that has shock collars around everyone so when they get angry or contentious and asocial, they're shocked into submission. You write that good TV writing starts with reading good writing. What happens to television if people are reading less? I really love words. I love the meaning of words, the sound of words, the music of words. And comedy, from my perspective, is really absolutely correct use of words to cause a response; to cause laughter. And laughter happens to you. Real laughter is involuntary. It should surprise the laugher. And that's a result of both words and images. I guess I could be concerned about a future where words become less relevant because they're my favorite things. Finally, some quick-fire questions. If you had to cast someone to portray you, who would you insist on? Idris Elba. No? Maybe not. (laughs) Why would you even ask that question? Are we going to make a movie out of the book? You never know! If you could revisit one of your shows, which would it be? "Dharma and Greg." I've always felt a profound regret for having left. There was so much more to explore, but I didn't know how. What’s your comfort watch? I really am drawn to dramas. I like to watch what I don't do. I love "Slow Horses" and "Furious." "Lucky" was another thing I saw and really enjoyed. "The Diplomat" is (also) terrific. As far as current comedies are concerned, if I want to laugh, I watch John Oliver and Jon Stewart. They absolutely know how to make me laugh out loud. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Le pape Léon XIV va quitter l'hôpital samedi
item.description: Le pape Léon XIV, qui a subi mardi une intervention chirurgicale pour le retrait d'un nodule pulmonaire cancéreux détecté à un stade précoce, quittera l'hôpital Gemelli de Rome samedi après-midi, annonce le Vatican.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV, qui a subi mardi une intervention chirurgicale pour le retrait d'un nodule pulmonaire cancéreux détecté à un stade précoce, quittera l'hôpital Gemelli de Rome samedi après-midi, annonce le Vatican. Le pape fera dimanche midi sa première apparition publique depuis son hospitalisation pour prononcer la traditionnelle prière de l'Angélus, a confirmé le Saint-Siège.

item.title: Pope Leo leaves hospital four days after lung cancer surgery
item.description: Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon to return to the Vatican following surgery for lung cancer four days ago.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon to return to the Vatican following surgery for lung cancer four days ago. The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. His doctors had earlier said he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging. The pope, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery on Sunday when he leads weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT). Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"raised questions"] about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness. The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.

item.title: Indian state food safety authority names Reliance, Blinkit executives in expired food probe
item.description: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi
item.content:encoded: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters. The Food and Drug Administration of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai, has led a [USN:L4N44Z0MR TEXT:"crackdown"] on food safety under its chief Tukaram Mundhe, 51, including shutting down some of Mumbai’s most popular eateries as well as outlets of Domino’s and Pizza Hut for poor hygiene. The state agency has also suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet. The latest case, which has led to a police complaint by the food safety authority, involves large retail and quick-commerce companies, which sell products to millions of households in the world’s most populous country. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, according to the documents reviewed by Reuters, said its officials visited some warehouses of Reliance Retail, Reliance Consumer and Zomato Hyperpure, and that company officials could not provide verifiable proof that disposal of expired food was actually carried out by their contractors. "The disposal agencies ... do not destroy the stock," the case document alleged. In the case of a Zomato Hyperpure warehouse, a company representative named a contractor as its disposal agency which FDA officials could not trace, according to the documents. Reliance and Blinkit did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Any attempt to divert expired, damaged or consumer-rejected food products meant for destruction back into the market is a serious matter that demands strict scrutiny and accountability," Maharashtra's FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters. "No company, brand, business or individual is above the law when it comes to food safety." INDIA'S INTENSIFYING CRACKDOWN Reliance Retail and Reliance Consumer are part of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s business group. Zomato’s Hyperpure is a unit of Eternal that also runs food delivery service Zomato and quick commerce business Blinkit. The FDA probe said it found a pattern where large retail and quick commerce distribution warehouses handed over expired and customer-rejected packages of food to contractors who passed the food to unlicensed sorting yards. These sorting yards then separated out saleable-looking packets, which eventually reached other retailers and the consumer market, according to case documents from the probe. "The chain thus runs from company warehouse to disposal agency, unlicensed yard, broker, retailer and consumer." The Maharashtra FDA on Thursday suspended the licences of five establishments in the state — three Reliance and two Eternal entities, the case documents said. Enforcement of food safety laws has traditionally been weak in India and the recent round of extensive crackdowns has garnered large-scale public support. In August, Indian authorities [USN:L4N44S18T TEXT:"raided"] an illegal operation in Mumbai that faked expiry dates and nutritional information on original food products manufactured by PepsiCo (PEP.O) , Nestle (NESN.S) , Coca-Cola (KO.N) and Unilever, so they could be exported to other countries. (This story has been corrected to say 'Reliance retail and consumer units,' not 'Reliance Group entities,' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
item.description: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030. Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act. Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery. He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion". Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"initial public offering"] expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion. HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control. "We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials. AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a [USN:L1N45Z01U TEXT:"source of growth"] offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash. Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind. But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants. More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said. STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology. "Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said. Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety." Despite some recent high-profile incidents where [USN:L4N45N1OZ TEXT:"rogue AI systems"] have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years." Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

item.title: India's HDFC Bank Q2 profit rises 4.7%; deputy MD Bharucha to step down
item.description: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank (HDBK.NS) , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth. The lender also said in a regulatory filing that its deputy managing director Kaizad Bharucha will step down at the end of December. The news comes days before a leadership change at the Mumbai-based lender. Anup Bagchi, a veteran of the ICICI group, takes over as managing director and CEO for three years from October 27, becoming HDFC Bank's first external chief executive. Bharucha, who has been with HDFC Bank for over three decades, was one of two contenders for the top job, Reuters had [USN:L4N44R00C TEXT:"reported"]. Bagchi [USN:L1N45N0I6 TEXT:"takes charge"] amid increased scrutiny of the bank's governance, profitability and operational performance. The lender posted a standalone net profit of 195.10 billion Indian rupees ($2.05 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, compared with 186.41 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts had estimated a profit of 195.26 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG. Treasury trading gains fell to 7.8 billion rupees from 23.9 billion rupees a year earlier, weighing on earnings despite broad-based loan growth. Other income, which includes gains on bonds and other investments, fell 3.6% to 138.31 billion rupees. Indian lenders reported strong credit growth in the quarter across corporate and retail loans. HDFC Bank's net interest income rose 9.7% to 346.19 billion rupees, with total loans up 16.3%. Deposits grew 18.8% from a year earlier, and the credit-to-deposit ratio stood at 96.0%. Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies rose 2.1% to 35.74 billion rupees. Asset quality improved. The gross non-performing asset ratio was 1.11% at the end of September, compared with 1.17% at the end of June. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: Un ministre russe au FMI boycotté par les Européens
item.description: Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes. "De nombreuses délégations ont quitté les lieux, dont des membres de l'Union européenne", a dit l'une des sources. Selon une deuxième source, une dizaine de délégués dont ceux du Danemark, de la Suède, de la Finlande, de la Norvège et des pays baltes ont quitté la pièce où se déroulait la réunion. "La guerre en Ukraine est existentielle pour nous en Europe", a déclaré un diplomate européen. "Nous ne pouvons pas normaliser nos relations avec la Russie." Jeudi, l'Allemagne a mis en garde contre les efforts visant à réintégrer la Russie au sein d'institutions internationales, après la participation d'Anton Silouanov à une réunion des ministres des Finances et banquiers centraux du G20 à Asheville, en Caroline du Nord, à la fin août. Les Etats-Unis, qui président pour l'heure le G20, avaient soutenu la présence du ministre russe en dépit de l'opposition des Européens. "Je constate des tentatives, notamment de la part des États-Unis (...) visant à ramener la Russie sur la scène internationale", a déclaré jeudi aux journalistes Lars Klingbeil, le ministre allemand des Finances. "Il est hors de question de faire comme si la Russie redevenait un membre normal du G20 et reprenait tout simplement sa place à la table, en tout cas, pas avec moi, ni avec les autres Européens." Les dirigeants de l'UE ont affiché vendredi, lors de leur sommet à Bruxelles, leur soutien au président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, objet depuis plusieurs jours de vives critiques de son homologue américain Donald Trump. Le locataire de la Maison blanche a conclu un accord la semaine dernière avec Moscou pour autoriser l'exportation de diesel russe et annoncé vendredi la levée de plusieurs sanctions, restrictions et droits de douane visant la Russie pourtant prévus dans le cadre d'une loi votée par le Congrès qu'il avait promulguée le mois dernier.

item.title: Rennie promises All Blacks will stick to their guns at World Cup
item.description: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his team would be sticking to their expansive style at next year's World Cup after the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Nick Mulvenney
item.content:encoded: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his team would be sticking to their expansive style at next year's World Cup after the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby on Saturday. Two convincing wins over Australia have got the three-times world champions back to winning ways after they lost a four-match series against South Africa 3-1. The Springboks have ridden a physical, conservative playing style to back-to-back World Cup triumphs but Rennie said he remained convinced the tactics that put a premium on ball speed and width would be effective against it. "There's no point playing this way and then going to a World Cup and trying to play risk-free footy," he told reporters after the 42-21 victory at Stadium Australia. "We're well aware you can put yourself under pressure the way that we're trying to play, but we'll also back ourselves that we'll profit more than we'll suffer in those situations. "I don't think you want all the teams in the world playing the same game. I think if you look at the Wallabies, they're pretty similar to us. I think they'll want to play, and it's a point of difference, part of the DNA of both sides." "If you want to just get into arm wrestles with a couple of the big sides in the world, it'll be a struggle," he said. Despite his team scoring six tries with some breathtaking rugby in the first half on Saturday, Rennie said there were still improvements to be made. "We're trying to grow our game, and we've got a long way to go," he said. "We just want to be able to play at a tempo that will test other sides." Australia coach Les Kiss said he was pleased with the performance of flyhalf Declan Meredith in only his fourth test and remained confident the Wallabies could put on a good showing at their home World Cup next year. "I've always said we'll have ups and downs, and today it was a bit of a downer again," he said. "But there are some good clues about what we're trying to do in our game. When we do play with footy in the hand with a positive intent, we're making a lot of breaks against one of the best teams in the world. "So I think there are some good qualities that are coming through. So I'm optimistic still."

item.title: ECB officials see December rate hike as uncertainty clouds 2027 outlook
item.description: Policymakers see December as the likeliest time for a rate increase, while rising bond yields, high energy costs, AI investment and uncertainty over US policy complicate the outlook for next year ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jana Randow and Alexander Weber European Central Bank officials are preparing to finish 2026 with a third interest-rate increase, the last before an increasingly complex backdrop overshadows decisions next year. While policymakers speaking this week in Bangkok kept open the option of acting in October, they pointed to December as the more likely timing for a hike that’s also widely anticipated among traders and economists. But the discussions also revealed growing unease over issues including rising bond yields, high energy costs and the blistering investment boom in artificial intelligence.  “The tradeoffs for monetary policy are going to get more tricky,” Governing Council member Martins Kazaks said in an interview. “So far, the decisions have been relatively easy. But there’s a lot of uncertainty and very low visibility.” The gathering in the Thai capital was dominated by warnings that the economy’s surprising resilience to the Middle East conflict will come under increasing strain. The euro zone, where investors have pushed up France’s borrowing costs due to its gaping budget deficit and political gridlock, was a focal point.  US midterm elections and an unpredictable response from President Donald Trump are adding to the uncertainty. Policymakers signaled a preference for sticking with a quarterly pace of rate increases, suggesting continuity after being the first major central bank to hike rates since the war broke out. That would mean waiting until the Dec. 17 gathering, when they’ll have new economic forecasts.  “From a policymaker’s perspective, you want to take decisions when you have the largest amount of data available, and the next such meeting is December,” Governing Council member Gediminas Simkus said in a separate interview. “But you also can’t ignore the fact that we have a meeting in October.” On the bright side, the Lithuanian and his colleagues pointed out that inflation heading toward 4 per cent — double the ECB’s target — hasn’t yet spread widely. At the same time, there are no signs that energy-driven price pressures are letting up.   On Friday, Brent oil hit $110 a barrel for the first time since May after Iran-backed Houthi rebels pummeled Saudi Arabia with missile and drone strikes, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged tit-for-tat attacks on energy infrastructure. With wage negotiations looming next spring, the ECB is carefully analyzing how such shocks are “traveling through the economy,” President Christine Lagarde told CNN. “We are not seeing any of that yet, but we have to be extremely careful that little signs, indices of such secondary effects are visible.”  Officials are already pondering how restrictive monetary policy needs to become. The last two hikes, in June and September, took the deposit rate to the upper end of the range the ECB previously identified as neutral.  Additional moves — traders are betting on three by September next year — would start to damp economic activity just as a long-awaited recovery is taking hold.   “The market is pricing that we are going to have to do more,” Governing Council member Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg TV. “It’s a base case that looks reasonable, but again, we are in a very uncertain world.” Some of that uncertainty is originating in Europe, with French finances in the spotlight after a bond-market selloff stoked memories of the sovereign-debt crisis that shook the region through much of the 2010s. Many participants in Bangkok, including IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva, argued that large budget deficits and debts must urgently be addressed, calling advanced economies the “worst offenders.”  While some ECB officials signaled optimism that the message investors sent to France has resonated with the government as it prepares key budget votes, others are already focused on how to respond if the situation deteriorates. “The toolbox allows for quite a lot of instruments,” said Governing Council member Martin Kocher. “We are not at the stage where we need to discuss any of these instruments. But they are there if they are needed.” The ECB’s work is overshadowed by increasing frustration among officials about Lagarde’s refusal to offer clarity on a possible early exit, according to people familiar with the matter.  The institution is in the midst of a major leadership overhaul, with Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel leaving in January, Chief Economist Philip Lane’s term expiring in May and Lagarde’s technically running through October 2027. Vice President Boris Vujcic joined in June.

item.title: Axis Bank Q2FY27 result: Profit rises 38% to ₹7,003 crore, misses estimates
item.description: Net interest income rose 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, while loans grew 23 per cent and provisions fell 52.2 per cent; other income declined 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore ...

Deposits increased 20.7 per cent from a year earlier.Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2 per cent to ₹1,694 crore.The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16 per cent at end-September, compared with 1.28 per cent three months earlier.

item.title: Une frappe russe fait un mort à Kherson, dans le sud de l'Ukraine - gouverneur
item.description: Une frappe aérienne russe sur la ville de Kherson dans le sud de l'Ukraine a fait un mort et 19 blessés samedi, déclare le gouverneur local sur la messagerie Telegram.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Une frappe aérienne russe sur la ville de Kherson dans le sud de l'Ukraine a fait un mort et 19 blessés samedi, déclare le gouverneur local sur la messagerie Telegram. La personne tuée était un ambulancier et un enfant figure parmi les blessés, a précisé Oleksandr Prokoudine. Dans la région russe de Belgorod, une femme a été tuée lors d'attaques de drones ukrainiens, rapporte l'agence Tass citant les secours.

item.title: Tanker struck by unknown projectile off Saudi Arabia on Friday, UKMTO says
item.description: An unknown projectile struck a tanker 68 nautical miles northeast of Saudi Arabia's Jubail on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in a report on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An unknown projectile struck a tanker 68 nautical miles northeast of Saudi Arabia's Jubail on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in a report on Saturday. All crew members were safe and had been evacuated, it said, adding that no environmental impact had been reported. UKMTO later issued a second report on Saturday that a tanker was attacked by a rocket-propelled grenade from a small boat 78 nautical miles northeast of Jubail on Friday, damaging its aft port quarter. All crew members were safe, it said, while the full extent of the damage and the environmental impact was not yet known. Reuters could not immediately establish whether the two reports referred to the same incident.

item.title: Russian defence ministry says it hit Ukrainian steel plants, power infrastructure overnight
item.description: Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian infrastructure targets, including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian infrastructure targets, including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih. The plant is owned by steel giant ArcelorMittal , which [USN:L1N45H03O TEXT:"suspended "]the facility's operations in September after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. In a statement, the ministry said the plant supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. It said Russian forces had also hit an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line. A cargo vessel in the Black Sea was also hit, it said, alleging that it was delivering military cargo to Ukraine's Odesa port. Reuters could not independently confirm the ministry's report.

item.title: India's Axis Bank quarterly profit rises 37.6%, but misses estimates on higher costs
item.description: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank (AXBK.NS) reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions. Axis Bank, the country's third-largest private bank by assets, posted a stand-alone net profit of 70.03 billion Indian rupees ($737.5 million) for the quarter ended on September 30, compared with 50.90 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts, on average, had forecast a profit of 71.24 billion rupees, according to LSEG-compiled data. Other income, which includes earnings from bonds and other investments, fell 1.4% to 65.31 billion rupees. Rising bond yields and volatility in the rupee during the quarter weighed on treasury income at the Mumbai-based lender, tempering earnings even as lending expanded across segments. Banks across India reported strong loan growth during the quarter across corporate and retail portfolios. Net interest income grew 11.8% to 153.71 billion rupees, helped by a 23% rise in total loans. Deposits increased 20.7% from a year earlier. Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2% to 16.94 billion rupees. The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16% at end-September, compared with 1.28% three months earlier. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: ECB's Lagarde says bond selloff will slow inflation
item.description: A selloff in bonds is making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Canepa
item.content:encoded: A selloff in bonds is making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde said on Saturday. Bond yields around the world have surged in recent weeks, with [USN:L1N46002V TEXT:"debt-laden France"] among the hardest hit, on the back of worries about debt and inflation as well as growing [USN:L1N4620D1 TEXT:"competition for credit"] from AI investments. Lagarde said this would make it harder than the ECB had projected last month for consumers to absorb higher fuel prices from the Iran war. "While growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting," Lagarde told fellow central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok. "This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise." The ECB has raised interested rates twice in the last four months and a further hike is expected in December, which would take its policy rate to 2.75% — a level it considers restrictive, or curtailing economic activity. Fellow ECB policymaker Joachin Nagel hinted at more policy tightening ahead, although he added that the central bank would decide at each meeting based on incoming data. "We are fighting against inflation, I'm of the opinion that the job is not done so far," the Bundesbank president told a DZ Bank event in the Thai capital. "I do see that maybe we have to do more." Speaking alongside Nagel, his Finnish colleague Olli Rehn said the ECB would watch out for "second-round effects" from energy inflation on other prices and wages. "There is no sign of second-round effects, but we will stay vigilant because they might creep in quietly like a cat in socks," Rehn said.

item.title: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
item.description: A young lawmaker demands as new future as protests rage in Tirana.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Marjana Koceku's life changed last year when Prime Minister Edi Rama hand-picked her to run for Albania's parliament, one of a legion of young lawmakers he hoped would become the face of his Socialist Party. This week, however, the 25-year-old, now an independent member of parliament, joined [USN:L1N4610AQ TEXT:"mass student protests"] calling for Rama to step down. Corruption, a lack of jobs and a general feeling that the government does not work for them have created a deep-seated anger that spilled over this week, when young protesters swarmed the capital Tirana, setting fire to government buildings and banks and hurling pavement stones at police. The government and the police have condemned the violence. According to police figures, 500 protestors have been detained, 330 of whom have been released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded. Albania's unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe, including in France, where high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities. YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE "The country is amazing, but ... the wrong policies that have been implemented by this political elite are completely against what the Albanian communities and Albanian citizens have been asking and seeking for so long," Koceku said during the protests on Friday as police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters nearby. Rama, a former basketball player, has been in power since 2013, half Koceku's life. He won a fourth term in elections last year but his administration has since been dogged by corruption scandals. Rama denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down. "Governments are changed through democratic elections and we had them last year, not through violence," he said. Still, the protests represent the biggest threat to his rule yet. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania's pristine southern coastline. The project, whose backers include US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"wrongfully sold"] for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wanted by prosecutors"] on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. He did not respond to requests for comment. That was not the only controversy for Rama's government. Last year, prosecutors alleged that his deputy prime minister was involved in [USN:L6N3ZC0BA TEXT:"doling out construction contracts"] to favoured companies, charges Rama and the deputy deny. "I didn't agree, especially with the policies that they were implementing against nature, and our land and our Albania," Koceku said. This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard. The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake. "Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government."

item.title: All Blacks thump Wallabies in Sydney on the back of brilliant first half
item.description: The All Blacks rode a first-half try blitz to a 43-21 victory over the Wallabies at Stadium Australia on Saturday, extending their win streak over their trans-Tasman-Sea rivals to 13 matches.
item.dc:creator: Nick Mulvenney
item.content:encoded: The All Blacks rode a first-half try blitz to a 43-21 victory over the Wallabies at Stadium Australia on Saturday, extending their win streak over their trans-Tasman-Sea rivals to 13 matches. With the Bledisloe Cup already safely in the cupboard for a 24th year after last week's 50-19 win in Auckland, New Zealand exploded out of the blocks and crushed all thoughts of an upset with six tries before the break. Despite losing Jordie Barrett to a calf injury before kickoff and another centre in Quinn Tupaea early on with a concussion, the All Blacks overwhelmed the Wallabies with power, pace and precision in the opening 40 minutes. "I'm really proud of the boys, the way we came out on that in that first half," said New Zealand captain Codie Taylor. "It was a real challenge for us this week to make sure that we backed up a really good performance from last week, and I thought we were awesome in that first 40." Australia showed some flashes of backline brilliance, particularly in the second half, but struggled to get hold of the ball for prolonged periods and were unable to match the accuracy or clinical finishing of the All Blacks. In a whirlwind of offloads, winger Josh Moorby, fullback Beauden Barrett, flanker Peter Lakai and replacement back Rieko Ioane all crossed in the first 26 minutes to give the visitors a quick-fire 22-0 lead. Wallabies flyhalf Declan Meredith did well to get a pass away in the tackle just before the half-hour mark to send Jeremy Williams over for a try but the lock was sin-binned at the other end of the field two minutes later. All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi immediately made the extra man count with his team's fifth try and Beauden Barrett added a sixth, his second, off an intercept to send New Zealand into the break with a 36-7 lead. Moorby faked out the defence for his second five-pointer within three minutes of the restart before the Wallabies finally finished off a backline move for fullback Tom Wright to go over. Australia were looking stronger with their replacements on the pitch, and Meredith almost scored a try after a scything break up the middle, then saved a try at the other end. A clever line dropout from Wright did result in a third Australia try in the 66th minute for replacement back Filipo Daugunu that delighted the majority of the crowd of 73,399. New Zealand were reduced to 14 men after Samisoni Taukei'aho went off injured, and went down to 13 when debutant Chay Fihaki was shown a yellow card but managed to hold out the Wallabies for the last few minutes. "I'm gutted," said Wallabies captain Harry Wilson. "When you give a team like the All Blacks a head start it's tough, and it's not good enough for this group. "We've got to be a lot better. It's been a very disappointing series, and we're going to have to regroup."

item.title: Jayawardene leaves role as Mumbai Indians head coach
item.description: Mahela Jayawardene has stepped down from his role as the Mumbai Indians head coach, the Indian Premier League team said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Mahela Jayawardene has stepped down from his role as the Mumbai Indians head coach, the Indian Premier League (IPL) team said on Saturday. In his first stint at Mumbai Indians from 2017 to 2022, the 49-year-old guided the side to three titles. However, the former Sri Lanka captain was not able to replicate that success after rejoining the side in 2024, with Mumbai Indians finishing fourth in 2025 and losing in the playoffs, before ending the league second-bottom in 2026. "Together, we have shared some unforgettable moments, overcome challenges and built something we can all be proud of," Jayawardene said in a statement. "I leave with immense pride in what we have achieved together and will always carry a special place in my heart for MI. I wish the team every success in the years ahead."

item.title: China AI supply-chain IPOs hold firm despite valuation pullback, Citi says
item.description: Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi banker working with Chinese companies said.
item.dc:creator: Selena Li
item.content:encoded: Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi (C.N) banker working with Chinese companies said. Despite recent [USN:L1N46118D TEXT:"valuation"] pullbacks on data centre companies, largely originating from the US market, future AI supply-chain listings would continue in Hong Kong, said Simon Yuan, Citi's head of China investment banking. Chinese companies plan to list in Hong Kong are cushioned by a roughly even split between domestic Chinese and international demand, Yuan, who also heads Citi’s financial institutions group in APAC, said on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok. The market is supported by a pool of local liquidity, with rising southbound capital from the Chinese mainland emerging as a key buying force, Yuan said. Still, "if the whole AI cycle turns in the US — and we have seen some volatility in the last few weeks — you will see an impact everywhere, Hong Kong included,” he warned. Many Chinese hardware players have proactively established manufacturing footprints outside mainland China, he said, which helps them better service global clients and mitigate geopolitical friction. Chinese hardware suppliers have benefited from the global AI infrastructure boom, gaining both sales volume growth and higher unit prices, Yuan said. Next year, the focus in Hong Kong's equity capital markets is expected to shift away from pure hardware, toward Chinese artificial intelligence models and application developers, he said. "But these companies need to have a proven business model. They need to show very strong growth and profitability," he said. Propelled by Chinese tech funding demand, 118 firms went public in Hong Kong in the first nine months of the year, raising HK$388 billion ($49.4 billion), up 106% year-on-year. ($1 = 7.8479 Hong Kong dollars) (This story has been corrected to say 'Yuan', not 'Yuen', throughout.)

item.title: インド警察、「ゴキブリ人民党」創設者を逮捕＝報道
item.description: [１７日 ロイター] -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
[１７日 ロイター] - インドの複数のメディアは１７日、若者中心の団体「ゴキブリ人民党（ＣＪＰ）」の創設者アビジート・ディプケ氏が警察に逮捕されたと報じた。

テレビ局ＮＤＴＶとインディア・トゥデーによると、ディプケ氏は治安の混乱を防ぐために逮捕され、１７日に特別行政治安判事の前に出頭する予定だ。

同氏は拘束されたＣＪＰ幹部２人を支援するため、１６日にデリーで抗議集会を開くよう呼びかけていた。集会には数百人が参加し、国旗を振って選挙管理委員長の辞任を求めた。

ディプケ氏は１６日、デリー中心部の住宅から出たところを拘束され、短い口論の後、パトカーに押し込まれて連れ去られた。警察はこれに先立ち、ディプケ氏と面会し、抗議活動を実施しないよう警告していた。

item.title: Winless Kings hope absent offense will return against streaking Bruins
item.description: The Los Angeles Kings will continue the search for their first victory of the season when they host the Boston Bruins on Saturday evening.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Los Angeles Kings will continue the search for their first victory of the season when they host the Boston Bruins on Saturday evening. The Kings are 0-3-2 through the first five games, which is tied for the third-longest season-opening skid in franchise history. The 1984-85 team began with nine winless games (including three ties), a year after the club started with six winless games (including two ties). "The belief is there in our group, but it's just not at all good enough right now," Kings forward Trevor Moore said. Los Angeles has scored one goal in each of its past three defeats. "We need to generate more offense," first-year Kings coach Peter Laviolette said. Los Angeles took 40 shots in its most recent loss, against the visiting Edmonton Oilers on Tuesday, but only got one past Devon Levi in a 4-1 setback. "We generated a lot of chances, enough chances, but I'd still like to see more in different areas from our group," Laviolette said. "It's not based on what they did or they didn't do. I thought that they did a lot (against the Oilers). I thought they played hard and they were in the offensive zone. It's more, for me, that we need to continue to look at it because we're not scoring enough." Only one Los Angeles player, Artemi Panarin, has more than one goal this season. Panarin has three. Adrian Kempe, who scored 36 goals last season and 35 in 2024-25, has one goal, as does Quinton Byfield, a 20-goal scorer the past three seasons. "I have a lot of belief that the players in the room that have scored 20 goals, 25 goals, 30 goals, 35 goals, 40 goals in their past, I believe that they're capable of doing that," Laviolette said. "It hasn't fallen for us. I think once it does, I think you start to gain a little bit of confidence from that as well." The Kings will be facing a Boston team that has won four in a row following a 4-2 road victory over the Anaheim Ducks on Friday night. The Ducks scored two goals in the final minute of the first period to take a 2-0 lead, but the Bruins chipped away behind a power play that went 3-for-4 and a penalty kill that finished 5-for-5. "They came out pretty hard. They had a lot of juice the first half of the game," Boston coach Marco Sturm said of the Ducks. "But also knowing, as a young team, it's tough to keep that tempo up for 60 minutes, and I was just hoping that they were going to slow down, and I think that's what happened." Boston's Frederic Brunet scored his first NHL goal on a fluttering slap shot from just inside the blue line that got through Anaheim goalie Lukas Dostal and started the comeback. "Probably the worst shot of my career," Brunet said. "I thought, 'There's no way that went in.' " Jeremy Swayman will start in goal against the Kings after Michael DiPietro made 25 saves against the Ducks for his first career NHL victory. DiPietro, 27, first appeared in the NHL in 2018-19, and he was playing in his sixth game and making his fourth start on Friday. "I've been with Mikey a couple years in Providence (of the AHL) and the way it just happened, me scoring my first NHL goal and him getting the first win, it's great," Brunet said. --Field Level Media

item.title: Knights carry hot streak into clash with struggling Penguins
item.description: A four-game road trip has gotten off to a rocky start for the Pittsburgh Penguins, who followed a 5-3 setback at Chicago on Tuesday with a 5-2 loss at Colorado on Friday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: A four-game road trip has gotten off to a rocky start for the Pittsburgh Penguins, who followed a 5-3 setback at Chicago on Tuesday with a 5-2 loss at Colorado on Friday night. Now comes the tough part. The Penguins next face the defending Western Conference champion Vegas Golden Knights in the second game of a back-to-back on Saturday in Las Vegas before heading to Salt Lake City to play the Central Division-leading Utah Mammoth on Monday. Pittsburgh, which has just one win in its past six games (1-4-1), got off to a good start against the Avalanche, taking a 2-0 lead in the first nine minutes on goals by Evgeni Malkin and Bryan Rust just 29 seconds apart. It was all Colorado after that. Led by Nathan MacKinnon's one goal and three assists, his 36th career game with four points or more, the Avalanche scored five unanswered goals, including three in the second period, to pull away for the easy win. Afterward, the key word making the rounds in the Penguins locker room was "consistency." "The first period we came out and we were doing a lot of the things I know this group is capable of when we're on," Pittsburgh coach Dan Muse said. "It's just the consistency throughout the entire game. We're going to look at it. It's going to be a quick turnaround here. We're going to have to turn that page quick." Penguins defenseman Erik Karlsson added, "I don't think we played particularly bad hockey. I think we just played a really good team. I think they capitalized on more chances than we did." The Penguins now play a Vegas team that leads the NHL with 14 points and is 4-1-0 at home. The Golden Knights have won two in a row and come in off a 6-2 victory over the visiting Calgary Flames on Thursday. Mark Stone led the way with his second career regular-season hat trick, and Jack Eichel added a short-handed goal and two assists to lead the Pacific Division leaders. Vegas, which has fallen behind 3-0 twice to start games this season, took control from the start against Calgary. The Golden Knights jumped out to a 2-0 lead on goals by Brett Howden and Eichel in the first period and led 3-1 after two periods before Stone capped the win with a natural hat trick in the third period. Stone leads the Golden Knights with six goals while Eichel is second with five to go along with a team-high 11 assists. "We were ready to play. It's nice to get one early there," first-year Vegas coach Ryan Craig said. "The short-handed goal, obviously with Jack making a great play and going in and scoring, nice to get up in that situation. Give our guys credit for being ready to go." Ivan Barbashev tied his career high with three assists and Carter Hart made 28 saves for the Golden Knights, who have won six of their past seven games. "Everybody's stepping up," Barbashev said. "It's fun to play right now. We're winning a lot of games, which makes it even more fun. Hopefully it continues the same way." --Field Level Media

item.title: Greenpeace activists occupy Woodside gas project unit off Western Australia
item.description: Greenpeace said on Saturday activists occupied a floating production unit at Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough gas project off the coast of Western Australia state.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Greenpeace said on Saturday activists occupied a floating production unit at Woodside's (WDS.AX) $12.5 billion Scarborough gas project off the coast of Western Australia state. Four activists scaled the unit and displayed banners with message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef", the environmental advocacy group said on its website. The protest temporarily shut down operations at the semi-submersible unit, Greenpeace said. Greenpeace is among environmental groups concerned about the project's potential impact on Scott Reef, a coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale located about 390 km (242 miles) off the state's northwest coast. Woodside in a statement said it was "responding to an incident involving individuals who have gained unlawful access to the Scarborough floating production unit". "Our immediate focus is on managing the situation safely and minimising risk to the individuals involved and our workforce," a Woodside spokesperson said. Australian Border Force said it was aware of protest activity off the Western Australian coast and was working with federal and state agencies in response. Woodside says it has conducted extensive environmental consultation on the project since 2018.

item.title: IMF members call for more support amid war shocks, 'advanced intelligence' risks
item.description: International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside. And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok. "Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," said the statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chair of the IMFC. The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender. Al-Jadaan told Reuters that the language of the statement was agreed by all members. Earlier this week, the United States was pressing fellow IMF members to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" in the statement, in line with US President Donald Trump's preferred name for the technology, a [USN:L1N4610GV TEXT:"senior US Treasury official told Reuters"]. The final version of the chair's statement contained no reference to artificial intelligence. It said the uncertain impact of "advanced intelligence technologies", along with rising bond yields in major economies that spill over to highly indebted economies, "could amplify macro-financial vulnerabilities." "Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the statement said. The member economies agreed to support countries that undertake reforms and address debt vulnerabilities, with specific attention to low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries and conflict-affected states. "We encourage increasing support to countries with sustainable debt and strong reform and growth enhancing agenda, but facing short-term financing challenges," the statement said, noting that several members had provided assurances of support to the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which supports poor and developing countries.

item.title: ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋
item.description:
Milana Vinn
[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋 15:08 配信

ソフトバンクグループのロゴ。９月東京で撮影。REUTERS/Manami Yamada

Milana Vinn

[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの買収を検討している。関係者が１６日明らかにした。買収案では、アライドの評価額が約１８０億ドルになる可能性がある。

アライドは企業や各種施設、大規模イベントに警備員を派遣する事業を手がける。データセンター分野でも事業を拡大しており、施設の開発と運営の両面を支援している。

ソフトバンクはアライドの買収が実現すれば、特定の警備業務で人員の一部をいずれロボットに置き換えることを目指す。ただ人型ロボットの警備業務への導入には長い時間がかかるとみられる。

買収検討は初期段階にあり、買収額を含め、最終決定には至っていないという。
